name: Administrative cooperation in taxation (DAC)
impact_assessment: No IA reviewed for the 2009 proposal; evaluations SWD(2019) 327 and COM(2025) 695
evidence_rating: moderate: two Commission evaluations with cost/benefit estimates, ECA audit, and causal evidence on the CRS (DAC2) deposit effect; benefit attribution remains weak
summary: The EU's tax-information exchange rules set no monitoring indicators. The Commission's 2025 evaluation estimates they raise about EUR 6.8 billion a year in tax against running costs of about EUR 646 million, mostly paid by business, though EU auditors found much exchanged data is poor quality or unused. Independent research on automatic bank-account exchange finds an 11.5% drop in deposits in tax havens, with some money moving to non-participating countries.

indicators.objective: The 2009 DAC proposal (COM(2009) 29) contains no financial-statement indicators; the Directive relies on five-yearly Commission reports under Article 27 and Member State statistics
Fight tax fraud, evasion and avoidance
indicators.indicator: Tax benefits generated by exchanged information
indicators.evidence: 2019 evaluation: benefits largely unmeasured; the few monetised estimates summed to about EUR 620m. 2025 evaluation: estimated benefits around EUR 6.8bn a year (EUR 1.2bn from automatic exchange under DAC1/DAC2, EUR 5.6bn from country-by-country reporting under DAC4), based on a contractor study and Member State estimates.

indicators.indicator: Costs to tax administrations and business
indicators.evidence: 2019: cumulative cost about EUR 230m (EUR 90m Member States, EUR 140m financial institutions). 2025: recurring costs about EUR 646m a year, EUR 604m borne by business (EUR 550m DAC2 reporting).

indicators.indicator: Matching and use rates of data received
indicators.evidence: 5-15% of DAC1-4 data still cannot be matched to taxpayers; Member States do not systematically monitor or publish outcomes (ECA 2021). TADEUS KPIs agreed but not binding.

Independent difference-in-differences study of the OECD Common Reporting Standard (implemented in the EU by DAC2) finds an 11.5% fall in cross-border deposits in tax havens, but relocation to non-participating jurisdictions (notably the US).

literature.citation: European Commission (2019), Evaluation of Council Directive 2011/16/EU on administrative cooperation in the field of taxation, SWD(2019) 327 (executive summary SWD(2019) 328)
literature.title: Evaluation of Council Directive 2011/16/EU on administrative cooperation in the field of taxation
literature.method: ex-post evaluation (Member State data 2013-2017, consultation, contractor study)
literature.headline: Limited evidence of effectiveness; cumulative costs about EUR 230m; the few monetised benefit estimates total about EUR 620m; monitoring failed to collect data on benefits
literature.summary_plain: The first evaluation found the tax-information exchange framework works, but data on its benefits were too thin to draw firm conclusions.

literature.citation: European Commission (2025), Report on the evaluation of Council Directive 2011/16/EU on administrative cooperation in the field of taxation, COM(2025) 695
literature.title: Report on the evaluation of Council Directive 2011/16/EU on administrative cooperation in the field of taxation
literature.method: ex-post evaluation (contractor study, Member State estimates)
literature.headline: Benefits estimated at about EUR 6.8bn a year against recurring costs of about EUR 646m (EUR 604m on business); DAC6 complex and inconsistently applied; 5-15% of data cannot be matched
literature.summary_plain: The Commission's second evaluation estimates the rules bring in about EUR 6.8 billion a year in tax, roughly ten times their running cost, though most of the cost falls on business.
literature.quality: Commission self-assessment; benefit attribution acknowledged to be difficult

literature.citation: European Court of Auditors (2021), Exchanging tax information in the EU: solid foundation, cracks in the implementation, Special Report 03/2021
literature.title: Exchanging tax information in the EU: solid foundation, cracks in the implementation
literature.headline: Framework well established but incomplete; information exchanged often of limited quality or underused; results not monitored
literature.summary_plain: EU auditors found the system sound in design, but much of the exchanged information is poor quality or unused, and nobody tracks the results.

literature.citation: Casi, Spengel & Stage (2020), Cross-border tax evasion after the common reporting standard: Game over?, Journal of Public Economics 190, 104240
literature.title: Cross-border tax evasion after the common reporting standard: Game over?
literature.headline: Automatic exchange under the CRS (implemented in the EU via DAC2) cut cross-border deposits in tax havens by 11.5%, but deposits relocated to non-participating jurisdictions, notably the US
literature.summary_plain: Automatic sharing of bank account data reduced money parked in tax havens by about 11.5%, but some of it simply moved to countries outside the scheme such as the US.
